legend: In this problem you will have to help Berland army with organizing their command delivery system.

There are n%%ZSMJ0%% officers in Berland army. The first officer is the commander of the army, and he does not have any superiors. Every other officer has exactly one direct superior. If officer a%%ZSMJ1%% is the direct superior of officer b%%ZSMJ2%%, then we also can say that officer b%%ZSMJ3%% is a direct subordinate of officer a%%ZSMJ4%%.
Officer x%%ZSMJ5%% is considered to be a subordinate (direct or indirect) of officer y%%ZSMJ6%% if one of the following conditions holds:
officer y%%ZSMJ7%% is the direct superior of officer x%%ZSMJ8%%;
the direct superior of officer x%%ZSMJ9%% is a subordinate of officer y%%ZSMJ10%%.
For example, on the picture below the subordinates of the officer 3%%ZSMJ11%% are: 5,6,7,8,9%%ZSMJ12%%.
The structure of Berland army is organized in such a way that every officer, except for the commander, is a subordinate of the commander of the army.

Formally, let's represent Berland army as a tree consisting of n%%ZSMJ13%% vertices, in which vertex u%%ZSMJ14%% corresponds to officer u%%ZSMJ15%%. The parent of vertex u%%ZSMJ16%% corresponds to the direct superior of officer u%%ZSMJ17%%. The root (which has index 1%%ZSMJ18%%) corresponds to the commander of the army.

Berland War Ministry has ordered you to give answers on q%%ZSMJ19%% queries, the i%%ZSMJ20%%-th query is given as (ui,ki)%%ZSMJ21%%, where ui%%ZSMJ22%% is some officer, and ki%%ZSMJ23%% is a positive integer.
To process the i%%ZSMJ24%%-th query imagine how a command from ui%%ZSMJ25%% spreads to the subordinates of ui%%ZSMJ26%%. Typical DFS (depth first search) algorithm is used here.

Suppose the current officer is a%%ZSMJ27%% and he spreads a command. Officer a%%ZSMJ28%% chooses b%%ZSMJ29%% — one of his direct subordinates (i.e. a child in the tree) who has not received this command yet. If there are many such direct subordinates, then a%%ZSMJ30%% chooses the one having minimal index. Officer a%%ZSMJ31%% gives a command to officer b%%ZSMJ32%%. Afterwards, b%%ZSMJ33%% uses exactly the same algorithm to spread the command to its subtree. After b%%ZSMJ34%% finishes spreading the command, officer a%%ZSMJ35%% chooses the next direct subordinate again (using the same strategy). When officer a%%ZSMJ36%% cannot choose any direct subordinate who still hasn't received this command, officer a%%ZSMJ37%% finishes spreading the command.
Let's look at the following example:
If officer 1%%ZSMJ38%% spreads a command, officers receive it in the following order: [1,2,3,5,6,8,7,9,4]%%ZSMJ39%%.
If officer 3%%ZSMJ40%% spreads a command, officers receive it in the following order: [3,5,6,8,7,9]%%ZSMJ41%%.
If officer 7%%ZSMJ42%% spreads a command, officers receive it in the following order: [7,9]%%ZSMJ43%%.
If officer 9%%ZSMJ44%% spreads a command, officers receive it in the following order: [9]%%ZSMJ45%%.

To answer the i%%ZSMJ46%%-th query (ui,ki)%%ZSMJ47%%, construct a sequence which describes the order in which officers will receive the command if the ui%%ZSMJ48%%-th officer spreads it. Return the ki%%ZSMJ49%%-th element of the constructed list or -1 if there are fewer than ki%%ZSMJ50%% elements in it.
You should process queries independently. A query doesn't affect the following queries.
input: The first line of the input contains two integers n%%ZSMJ51%% and q%%ZSMJ52%% (2≤n≤2⋅105,1≤q≤2⋅105%%ZSMJ53%%) — the number of officers in Berland army and the number of queries.

The second line of the input contains n−1%%ZSMJ54%% integers p2,p3,…,pn%%ZSMJ55%% (1≤pi<i%%ZSMJ56%%), where pi%%ZSMJ57%% is the index of the direct superior of the officer having the index i%%ZSMJ58%%. The commander has index 1%%ZSMJ59%% and doesn't have any superiors.

The next q%%ZSMJ60%% lines describe the queries. The i%%ZSMJ61%%-th query is given as a pair (ui,ki%%ZSMJ62%%) (1≤ui,ki≤n%%ZSMJ63%%), where ui%%ZSMJ64%% is the index of the officer which starts spreading a command, and ki%%ZSMJ65%% is the index of the required officer in the command spreading sequence.
output: Print q%%ZSMJ66%% numbers, where the i%%ZSMJ67%%-th number is the officer at the position ki%%ZSMJ68%% in the list which describes the order in which officers will receive the command if it starts spreading from officer ui%%ZSMJ69%%. Print "-1" if the number of officers which receive the command is less than ki%%ZSMJ70%%.
You should process queries independently. They do not affect each other.
